Capabilities and evidence

Source: vignettes/capabilities.Rmd
capabilities.Rmd

A solver needs to know things about an operator that it cannot afford to find out. Conjugate gradients converges on a Hermitian positive definite operator and can silently produce nonsense on one that is neither, and checking positive definiteness costs more than the solve. So the operator has to carry the claim.

The moment it carries a claim, a second question arrives: on whose word. A property established by construction, one measured exactly on stored data, one asserted by whoever wrote the adapter, and one guessed from ten random probes are all “positive definite is TRUE”, and they are not interchangeable. This vignette is about keeping the two apart and keeping both correct through the algebra.

Installation 

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/linop")

Installing linop installs one package. There are no Imports and no compiled code, so there is no toolchain to have working first. Matrix sits in Suggests and is used for sparse leaves and as_sparse().

R 4.4.0 or newer. The floor is set by crossprod() and tcrossprod(), which became S3 generic in R 4.4.0, and are what let one matrixOps method cover all three matrix products.

Ten capabilities, three values 

caps <- c("hermitian", "symmetric", "positive_definite", "positive_semidefinite",
          "unitary", "diagonal", "triangular_upper", "triangular_lower",
          "full_rank", "real")

hermitian and symmetric are separate entries. For a complex operator A = A^H and A = A^T are different statements, and a solver that takes one for the other takes a wrong branch. For a real operator they coincide, and the package records that coincidence as a rule instead of merging the fields.

Each capability holds TRUE, FALSE or NA. NA means unknown, and it is never read as FALSE.

S <- linop(function(X) X[c(2, 1), , drop = FALSE],
           adjoint = function(X) X[c(2, 1), , drop = FALSE],
           dim = c(2, 2))
cap(S, "positive_definite")
#> NA  (<none>)

That operator is a swap. It is Hermitian and it is not positive definite, and linop says neither, because nothing has established either one. Propagation is conservative in the same direction: a rule that cannot prove TRUE returns NA and never FALSE.

cap() reads one entry. summary() reads them all:

A <- linop(matrix(c(2, 1, 0,
                    1, 3, 1,
                    0, 1, 2), 3, 3))
summary(A)$caps[, c("capability", "value")]
#>               capability value
#> 1              hermitian  TRUE
#> 2              symmetric  TRUE
#> 3      positive_definite    NA
#> 4  positive_semidefinite    NA
#> 5                unitary    NA
#> 6               diagonal FALSE
#> 7       triangular_upper FALSE
#> 8       triangular_lower FALSE
#> 9              full_rank    NA
#> 10                  real  TRUE

The dense leaf filled those in by checking the stored matrix exactly. Symmetry came from all.equal(M, t(M)), diagonality from testing the off-diagonal entries. Positive definiteness is absent because establishing it would have cost a factorisation the constructor did not run.

Evidence is three independent fields 

evidence(source = "computation", guarantee = "identity", confidence = 1)
#> computation / identity / conf 1

source is where the claim came from: construction, adapter_contract, user_declaration, probe, computation, theorem.

guarantee is the kind of statement being made: identity, deterministic_bound, probabilistic_bound, estimate, heuristic.

confidence is 1, a stated probability, or NA.

The three are independent on purpose, and none of them is a rank. A randomised trace estimator carries a probabilistic_bound with a rigorous confidence; a deterministic heuristic carries no bound at all; an adapter contract can be worth more than a hundred probes. Collapsing that into one “strength” number loses exactly the distinctions a solver needs.

The fourth field is what makes it work: depends_on, a list of the evidence a rule relied on. It is empty when the rule is unconditional.

Declaring what you know

properties takes a named logical vector and records each entry as a user declaration.

P <- linop(function(X) X, adjoint = function(X) X, dim = c(4, 4),
           properties = c(hermitian = TRUE, positive_definite = TRUE))
cap(P, "positive_definite")
#> TRUE  (user_declaration / identity / conf 1)

A bare character vector is shorthand for all-TRUE, and an unknown name is an error naming the ten that exist.

linop(matrix(1:4, 2, 2), properties = c(hermitiann = TRUE))
#> Error:
#> ! unknown properties: hermitiann
#>   known: hermitian, symmetric, positive_definite, positive_semidefinite, unitary, diagonal, triangular_upper, triangular_lower, full_rank, real

Some implications hold by definition and are closed once at construction, so declaring the strong form does not oblige you to also declare the weak one:

cap(P, "positive_semidefinite")
#> TRUE  (construction / identity / conf 1 <- [user_declaration / identity / conf 1])

Positive definite implies positive semidefinite; diagonal implies both triangularities; a real Hermitian operator is symmetric and the converse. Each closure records what it depended on. A "double" operator is real by construction, unconditionally.

cap(linop(matrix(1:4, 2, 2)), "real")
#> TRUE  (construction / identity / conf 1)

Declaring hermitian or symmetric on a non-square operator is an error rather than a stored contradiction:

linop(matrix(1:6, 2, 3), properties = c(symmetric = TRUE))
#> Error:
#> ! a hermitian or symmetric operator must be square

Propagation

Every composite recomputes its capabilities from its operands. The rules are sound in the direction that matters: they claim TRUE only where the conclusion follows, and answer NA everywhere else.

Sums. hermitian, symmetric, positive_definite, positive_semidefinite, real, diagonal and both triangularities survive addition when every term has them.

D1 <- linop_scaling(c(1, 2, 3))
D2 <- linop_scaling(c(4, 5, 6))
cap(D1 + D2, "diagonal")$value
#> [1] TRUE
cap(D1 + D2, "positive_definite")$value
#> [1] TRUE

Scaling. A real scalar preserves hermitian; any scalar preserves symmetric; a positive real scalar preserves definiteness. A nonzero scalar preserves full_rank, and structure such as diagonal survives any scalar.

Pd <- linop(function(X) X, adjoint = function(X) X, dim = c(3, 3),
            properties = c(hermitian = TRUE, positive_definite = TRUE))

cap(2 * Pd, "positive_definite")$value
#> [1] TRUE
cap(-2 * Pd, "positive_definite")$value    # the rule cannot conclude
#> [1] NA
cap(-2 * Pd, "hermitian")$value            # a real scalar keeps this one
#> [1] TRUE

A diagonal leaf answers FALSE to the same question, and the difference is worth understanding. Scaling a diag is a simplification rule: the result is a fresh diagonal leaf, whose constructor computes definiteness exactly from the stored vector rather than inheriting a propagated claim.

cap(-2 * D1, "positive_definite")$value
#> [1] FALSE
(-2 * D1)$node
#> [1] "diag"

Transpose, adjoint, conjugate. adjoint() preserves hermitian, definiteness, unitary, diagonal, full_rank and real, and preserves symmetric when the operand is also real. t() preserves symmetric and preserves hermitian when the operand is real. Both flip the triangularities. Conj() preserves everything.

U <- linop(matrix(c(1, 0, 2, 1), 2, 2))      # upper triangular
cap(U, "triangular_upper")$value
#> [1] TRUE
cap(t(U), "triangular_upper")$value
#> [1] NA
cap(t(U), "triangular_lower")$value
#> [1] TRUE

Products. A product of two arbitrary operators tells you nothing, and the rules say so. Two exceptions are structural, and they hold whatever is known about the operand:

K <- linop(matrix(rnorm(12), 4, 3))
G <- adjoint(K) %*% K
cap(G, "hermitian")
#> TRUE  (construction / identity / conf 1)
cap(G, "positive_semidefinite")$value
#> [1] TRUE
cap(G, "positive_definite")$value            # NA until K is known full rank
#> [1] NA

adjoint(X) %*% X is Hermitian and positive semidefinite for every X, so the evidence has nothing underneath it. Positive definiteness needs X to have full rank, so it appears only when that is known, and then it records the dependency.

The product node finds this by structural recognition, comparing the two factors rather than testing the result. It is conservative: it may fail to notice that two separately built operators are equal, and it never claims that two different operators are the same.

Kr <- linop(matrix(rnorm(12), 4, 3))
cap(crossprod(Kr), "symmetric")$value        # t(A) A is symmetric for any A
#> [1] TRUE
cap(crossprod(Kr), "hermitian")$value        # and Hermitian too, since A is real
#> [1] TRUE

For a complex operator the two come apart, which is the point of keeping them separate:

Kz <- linop(matrix(c(1 + 1i, 2, 0, 3 - 2i), 2, 2))
cap(crossprod(Kz), "symmetric")$value        # A^T A is symmetric
#> [1] TRUE
cap(crossprod(Kz), "hermitian")$value        # and is not Hermitian
#> [1] NA
cap(adjoint(Kz) %*% Kz, "hermitian")$value   # A^H A is
#> [1] TRUE

Structure that survives any product is carried through: a product of diagonals is diagonal, of upper triangulars is upper triangular, of unitaries is unitary, of reals is real.

cap(D1 %*% D2, "diagonal")$value
#> [1] TRUE

The case this design exists for

Take two operators whose author declared them positive definite. The sum rule is unconditionally sound. So the sum is positive definite, by construction:

P <- linop(function(X) X, adjoint = function(X) X, dim = c(4, 4),
           properties = c(hermitian = TRUE, positive_definite = TRUE))
Q <- linop(function(X) 2 * X, adjoint = function(X) 2 * X, dim = c(4, 4),
           properties = c(hermitian = TRUE, positive_definite = TRUE))

cap(P + Q, "positive_definite")
#> TRUE  (construction / identity / conf 1 <- [user_declaration / identity / conf 1; user_declaration / identity / conf 1])

Read the evidence. The source is construction, which is true and is not the whole story: underneath it sit the two user declarations the rule consumed. Had the composite reported a bare construction, two unverified assertions would have been laundered into a fact by one addition, and a solver reading only the top-level source would accept them.

Requirements

A solver states what it will accept. The statement is a predicate over evidence, not a threshold on a strength number.

strict <- requirement(sources = c("construction", "computation", "theorem"),
                      guarantees = "identity")

evidence_satisfies() checks the evidence against it, and recurses into depends_on, so a requirement the inputs would have failed is failed by anything built from them.

evidence_satisfies(cap(P, "positive_definite")$evidence, strict)
#> [1] FALSE
evidence_satisfies(cap(P + Q, "positive_definite")$evidence, strict)
#> [1] FALSE

The Gram matrix passes the same requirement, because there is nothing underneath its evidence to fail it:

evidence_satisfies(cap(G, "positive_semidefinite")$evidence, strict)
#> [1] TRUE

A solver willing to take the author’s word says so explicitly, and then the same chain passes:

lenient <- requirement(sources = c("construction", "computation", "theorem",
                                   "user_declaration"))
evidence_satisfies(cap(P + Q, "positive_definite")$evidence, lenient)
#> [1] TRUE

min_confidence adds a numeric floor, applied at every level of the chain:

probabilistic <- evidence("probe", "probabilistic_bound", confidence = 0.99)
evidence_satisfies(probabilistic, requirement(min_confidence = 0.999))
#> [1] FALSE
evidence_satisfies(probabilistic, requirement(min_confidence = 0.95))
#> [1] TRUE

This is the shape of the contract Phase 2 solvers will use: CG will require Hermitian positive definiteness under a requirement it publishes, and an operator whose claim rests on an unverified declaration will be turned away by name rather than converge to something wrong.

Probing a declaration

verify() tests declared capabilities against the operator’s actual behaviour. Agreement is recorded beside the declaration as a probe and never promoted to proof; a contradiction fails the certificate.

Good <- linop(function(X) X, adjoint = function(X) X, dim = c(4, 4),
              properties = c(hermitian = TRUE))
verify(Good)$probes
#>   capability claimed gap    verdict
#> 1  hermitian    TRUE   0 consistent
#> 2  symmetric    TRUE   0 consistent
Liar <- linop(function(X) rbind(X[-1, , drop = FALSE], 0),
              adjoint = function(X) rbind(0, X[-4, , drop = FALSE]),
              dim = c(4, 4), properties = c(hermitian = TRUE))
verify(Liar)$probes
#>   capability claimed      gap      verdict
#> 1  hermitian    TRUE 1.664972 contradicted
#> 2  symmetric    TRUE 3.203087 contradicted
verify(Liar)$overall
#> [1] "fail"

Positive definiteness is the one case where a probe can only ever disagree. A positive Rayleigh quotient on ten random vectors is not evidence of definiteness, so the check looks for a negative one and reports consistent otherwise. The certificate records the guarantee as heuristic for exactly this reason.
